audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Wednesday, July 1st, 2026 — Canada Day. Here's what actually matters today, beneath the celebrations.

Let's start with the international student file, because the signals today are particularly useful for your consulting work.

First, Australia has done you a favour. The Australian government just announced another round of student visa fee increases, and the sector backlash has been fierce. Australian higher-education bodies are publicly saying — and I'm quoting directly — "competitor countries will be celebrating." And they're right. Canada, the UK, Germany, they're all positioned to absorb students who might have otherwise chosen Australia. But here's the nuance that's worth sitting with: Canada is only going to capture that advantage if it can tell a compelling, credible story to prospective students.

Which brings us to the second story, and it's more sobering. Canadian officials — including the envoy to India — are actively out there saying this is the "best time ever" to apply for a Canadian study visa. And on paper, they're not wrong. The PGWP pathways have stabilised somewhat, caps are clearer, the political climate toward immigration shifted after the last election cycle. But India Today is reporting that Indian students are not convinced. They're hesitant. The concerns aren't primarily about visa fees — they're about post-graduation employment outcomes, social climate, and whether the Canadian brand still delivers on its promise. That is a marketing and messaging problem, not a policy problem. And that is squarely in your lane.

Think about what this means for your consulting pipeline. Every Canadian university that depends on international enrolment — which is most of them — has a brand credibility gap right now in the Indian market specifically. The official government recruitment messaging isn't landing the way officials hope. The institutions that figure out how to speak authentically to Indian student concerns, through the right channels and with the right proof points, are going to outperform their peers in enrolment. That's a consulting engagement. The universities that dismiss it as a policy fix will fall behind. If you're building your higher-ed client pipeline, the international student recruitment and retention brief is your sharpest point of entry right now, and today's news hands you a concrete conversation-starter.

Now, on the AI front — two developments that deserve your attention, for different reasons.

The United Nations, through its International Telecommunication Union, is launching what it's calling the AI for Good Global Commission. First meeting is July 8th in Geneva. The lineup is notable: Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff is in the room, alongside heads of state including Rwanda's president. The explicit mandate is to connect the executives building advanced AI with global political leaders to forge some kind of shared governance framework.

Why does this matter to you specifically? Because one of the persistent challenges in selling AI-in-marketing consulting services is that your clients — especially risk-averse institutional clients like Canadian universities — are nervous about AI governance. They want to know there are guardrails. A credible UN-backed commission with real corporate and political participation changes the conversation. It gives you a reference point when you're sitting across from a cautious VP of Communications at a university saying, "there is a serious global governance apparatus emerging around this." It's not the Wild West anymore. That's a useful narrative shift.

The second AI story is more immediately practical. Anthropic just launched Claude Science — a purpose-built version of their Claude model specifically optimised for scientific research and pharmaceutical industry workflows. This is a meaningful milestone in AI productisation. What it demonstrates is that the era of one-size-fits-all AI tools is ending quickly. Domain-specific AI applications are arriving — not just for pharma and science, but the same logic will apply to marketing, to higher education, to real estate. When you're developing your AI-in-marketing consulting frameworks, the Claude Science launch is a useful reference: it shows clients that AI isn't just a generic productivity layer, it's becoming a specialised strategic capability. That framing elevates the conversation from "should we use ChatGPT" to "how do we build AI into our core workflows in a way that's designed for our domain."

Three strong marketing stories today, and together they paint a picture that's worth synthesising.

Start with Ulta's CMO Kelly Mahoney, who sat down with Marketing Dive to break down how the beauty retailer is actually driving growth. The playbook she describes is interesting precisely because it's not one thing — it's a layered system. Cultural partnerships to build brand heat. TikTok Shop for commerce-at-the-moment-of-inspiration. Retail media for performance. And it all sits under a coherent brand architecture. The reason this is worth your time is that the Ulta model is a template for how mid-to-large consumer brands should be thinking about omnichannel right now. If you're ever building a consulting deck on integrated marketing strategy — and you will be — the Ulta case study is clean, current, and credible.

Second, Adweek is asking the $1 trillion question: why are brands still massively underinvesting in women's sports? The answer, as the piece frames it, is inertia and outdated audience assumptions. The data on ROI is there. The audiences are there. The cultural moment — particularly in a World Cup year where Canada's national team has had a historic run — is absolutely there. And brands are still hesitating. This is a direct opportunity signal. If you have any clients in consumer marketing, the women's sports sponsorship brief is a legitimate strategic gap you could walk them into. The pitch practically writes itself: "Here is a documented $1 trillion underserved opportunity, here is the audience data, here is the activation framework."

Which connects neatly to the third story. Nike is already thinking about what comes after the World Cup ends. Their brand leadership is publicly talking about how to sustain the emotional momentum once the tournament is over. This is sophisticated brand lifecycle thinking — how do you prevent the post-event emotional hangover, how do you convert tournament-generated affinity into durable brand relationships? For you, as someone building a consulting practice, this is worth studying not just as a Nike case study but as a framework. Every major campaign or moment has a "what comes next" problem. The brands that plan for it win. The brands that don't leave value on the table.

Two real estate stories today that are worth brief but genuine attention.

First, HousingWire is reporting on what they're calling the end of the amenity arms race in multifamily real estate. For years, apartment buildings competed by bundling in increasingly elaborate shared amenities — gyms, rooftop pools, co-working lounges — all included in rent. Now, facing fee regulations and tighter margins, operators are converting those spaces into opt-in, revenue-generating profit centres. Pay for what you use. This is a structural shift in how income properties are managed and monetised, and it's a model that will migrate north. If you're thinking about any of your BC properties from an investment or management lens, this is the direction the industry is heading.

Second, there's an important piece about seniors holding a record share of housing wealth in North America, while the mortgage underwriting system hasn't caught up. Americans 70 and older now hold more real estate wealth than the 40-to-54 cohort — and Canadians 62-plus are sitting on comparable equity positions. The problem is that traditional mortgage underwriting still struggles to assess retiree income and assets consistently, which blocks equity access. This matters because as you think about your own property portfolio across Sun Peaks, Langley, and Vancouver over the long term, understanding how equity access frameworks are evolving is directly relevant to how you plan transitions, renovations, or investment decisions down the road.

Locally, three things worth knowing on Canada Day.

The headline you'll want to know as a Sun Peaks property owner: the resort is hosting its first-ever Heartland Country Festival. It's a new event, which means it will bring foot traffic and energy to the mountain this weekend. Worth being aware of if you're heading up, or if you're tracking short-term rental activity on your property.

On a more serious note, Kamloops RCMP are actively seeking a person of interest following a suspicious house fire in Brocklehurst. It's an open investigation and a public safety matter — worth monitoring if you have family in that part of the city.

And in a significant local governance development, Kamloops city council has formally backed Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc's bid to add Highway 5 properties to their reserve. This affects the corridor between Kamloops and Sun Peaks directly — any changes to land status along that highway have long-term implications for development, access, and the broader relationship between the city and the Tk'emlúps nation. It's a story to track over time, not just a one-day item.

Briefly on the global front — the CUSMA trade deadline passed today without a deal. Canadian, Mexican, and American negotiators were set to meet virtually on July 1st to continue talks on the Canada-US-Mexico Agreement. No resolution. The practical implication is continued uncertainty on cross-border trade costs, supply chains, and regulatory alignment. For anyone running a Canadian business or advising organisations with US exposure — which increasingly includes universities competing for American students and research funding — this prolonged ambiguity is a background risk that isn't going away soon. Keep it on your radar.

One story in the longevity category today, and it's an important one to flag even though it's not about your personal health directly.

STAT News is running a commentary from two leading epidemiologists arguing that the ongoing Ebola and Marburg outbreaks are exposing a fundamental structural gap in global pandemic preparedness. Their core argument is that we keep building diagnostic systems for specific, known pathogens — and that approach will always leave us flat-footed when the next novel threat emerges. What's needed, they argue, is pathogen-agnostic diagnostic infrastructure: systems that can detect an unknown threat quickly, not just identify a known one. This is a systems-thinking argument about public health, and it's the kind of long-range preparedness framing that tends to get ignored until the next crisis makes it obvious. File it as a reminder that pandemic risk hasn't disappeared — it's just quiet right now.

That's your Canada Day briefing, Midya. The through-line today is really about credibility gaps and strategic openings: Canada's international student recruitment messaging isn't landing the way officials hope, and that's a real consulting opportunity for you with Canadian universities. The AI governance conversation is maturing in ways that help you sell AI-in-marketing services to risk-averse institutional clients. And the marketing stories today — Ulta, women's sports, Nike's post-event strategy — together map out where smart brand strategy is heading. Enjoy the holiday where you can. The work will be waiting Thursday.
